7700:
To hoist something means to lift it upward, usually with effort, and often using a rope, chain, pulley, crane, or some other mechanical tool. The key idea is that the thing being lifted is heavy, large, or awkward enough that you can't just pick it up with your bare hands the way you'd pick up a pencil. There is a sense of deliberate, effortful raising.

Think of a sailor pulling a rope to raise a flag to the top of a tall pole. That's hoisting. The flag goes up, hand over hand, rope by rope, until it reaches the top and flies proudly. That physical image — something being pulled upward, purposefully and with some exertion — is the heart of the word.

These three words are close cousins, but hoist has its own personality.

Lift is the most general word. You can lift a feather, lift a finger, lift a baby. It asks nothing about how heavy the object is or how you're doing it.

Raise is also general. You raise your hand, raise the volume, raise a child. It focuses on the result (something goes higher) more than the effort.

Hoist is more specific. It quietly suggests:

  • The object is heavy or unwieldy.
  • The action requires real effort or mechanical assistance.
  • The movement is upward (not sideways).
  • There is often a sense of displaying the object once it's at the top.

So while you'd lift a cup off a table and raise your eyebrows, you'd hoist a heavy crate onto a truck or hoist a flag up a pole.

1. Flags and Banners

This is perhaps the most classic use. Countries, ships, and teams hoist their flags — they raise them up a pole or mast, usually as a symbol of pride, identity, or authority.

The soldiers hoisted the national flag at dawn.

2. Ships and Sailing

On ships, sailors hoist sails, cargo, and anchors. Because ships deal with very heavy equipment and require ropes and pulleys to move things, "hoist" fits naturally.

The crew hoisted the sails as the wind picked up.
The crane hoisted the cargo container onto the deck.

3. Heavy Objects and Construction

At building sites or warehouses, workers hoist beams, crates, machines, and equipment using cranes or pulleys.

Workers hoisted the steel beam to the top floor.

4. A Person's Own Body

Sometimes, a person hoists themselves up onto something — a wall, a ledge, a bar — implying they heave their own weight upward with effort.

He grabbed the ledge and hoisted himself up onto the roof.
She hoisted herself out of the swimming pool.

5. Lifting a Glass (Informal/Festive)

In a casual or celebratory context, people sometimes say someone hoisted a glass — meaning they raised a drink for a toast. This is a light, somewhat playful use.

They hoisted their glasses and toasted to the new year.

An important shade of meaning: hoist carries weight (pun intended). When you use this word, you're telling your reader that the lifting wasn't casual or easy. Compare:

  • She lifted the book off the table. → Easy, ordinary.
  • She hoisted the box onto the shelf. → Heavy, required effort.

If you describe someone hoisting something light, it would sound odd or even humorous, because the word sets an expectation of struggle.

Here are the natural ways "hoist" appears in sentences:

  • Hoist + object: They hoisted the anchor.
  • Hoist + object + up: He hoisted the bag up onto his shoulder.
  • Hoist + object + onto/over/into: The workers hoisted the engine into the truck.
  • Hoist + yourself + up/onto/over: She hoisted herself up over the fence.
The Famous Idiom: "Hoist by Your Own Petard"

You will likely come across this phrase one day, so it's worth knowing. It means to be harmed, trapped, or defeated by your own plan or trick — essentially, your scheme backfires and hurts you instead of the person you were targeting.

A "petard" was a small explosive device used in old warfare to blow open doors or walls. If it went off too early, the engineer who set it could be "hoisted" (blown upward) by his own bomb. The phrase preserves that dark irony beautifully.

He tried to spread rumors about his rival, but the truth came out and he ended up being hoisted by his own petard — his own reputation was destroyed instead.

You might also see the modern variation "hoist with your own petard" — both mean the same thing.

ConceptDetail

To hoist is to lift something heavy upward, typically with rope, a machine, or significant bodily effort. It's most at home with flags on poles, cargo on ships, and heavy loads at construction sites, but it also works when a person heaves their own body up onto something. It's always upward, always effortful, and often implies the object is being raised to a position where it will be seen, used, or secured. The key idiom to remember is "hoist by your own petard" — your plan blows up in your face.
7701:
Something is hokey when it feels fake, cheap, or embarrassingly oversimplified — especially when it's trying to seem meaningful, impressive, or emotional, but falls flat because it's too obvious, too clichéd, or too poorly put together to be convincing.

Think of it as the feeling you get when something insults your intelligence a little — not because it's evil or wrong, but because it's just… too easy. Too neat. Too manufactured.

There are a few overlapping qualities that the word captures:

1. Fake or artificial in an obvious way
When something is supposed to look or feel real, but you can clearly see it's not — and the attempt is kind of embarrassing. For example, a haunted house at a school fair where the "ghosts" are kids wearing white bedsheets and plastic fangs. It's supposed to be scary, but it's so obviously cheap and phony that it just makes you smile instead.

2. Overly sentimental in a cheap, manipulative way
When something tries to make you feel a strong emotion — moved, inspired, patriotic, teary-eyed — but does it in such a heavy-handed, unsubtle way that it feels hollow rather than genuine. Imagine a movie where the hero's dog dies in slow motion while sad piano music plays for two full minutes. The film is telling you to cry rather than earning that emotion honestly. That's hokey.

3. Clichéd and unoriginal
When something relies on tired, worn-out ideas, phrases, or plot devices that everyone has already seen a hundred times, so it feels lazy and predictable. A motivational poster that says "Reach for the stars!" in curly font over a picture of a sunset — hokey. A movie where the villain monologues long enough for the hero to escape — hokey.

4. Unsophisticatedly naïve
When something is so simple, so uncritically cheerful, or so oblivious to nuance that it feels a bit silly to a thoughtful adult. Old TV commercials where a smiling family magically solves all their problems by switching to a new brand of cereal have a hokey quality — life just doesn't work that cleanly.
The key nuance: hokey ≠ always bad

This is important. "Hokey" doesn't always mean something is terrible or worthless. In fact, people often use the word affectionately.

You can say: "It's hokey, but I love it."

This means: "Yes, it's cheap, corny, and unsophisticated — but I find it charming anyway." Nostalgia plays a big role here. Old monster movies with rubber suits, a small town's Fourth of July parade, your grandmother's sentimental fridge magnets — these things can be hokey and beloved at the same time. The hokeyness itself becomes part of the charm.

So "hokey" sits somewhere between gentle mockery and warm amusement. It's rarely a harsh insult — it's more of a knowing, slightly affectionate eye-roll.

• "The ending of that film was so hokey — everyone hugged, it started snowing, and a rainbow appeared. I almost laughed."
  • "The magician's tricks were hokey — you could clearly see the card up his sleeve."
  • "I know the team-building exercise seems hokey, but just go with it."
  • "Those old sci-fi special effects look hokey today, but back then people were amazed."
  • "She gave a hokey speech full of phrases like 'follow your dreams' and 'believe in yourself.'"
Words that are close in meaning

These are words that overlap with "hokey," each with a slightly different flavor:

  • Corny — very similar; cheap sentimentality or humor that's embarrassingly obvious
  • Cheesy — low quality in a way that feels tacky or in poor taste
  • Kitschy — cheap or garish in taste, often applied to décor or art
  • Schmaltzy — excessively and artificially sentimental (stronger focus on emotion)
  • Contrived — artificially constructed; not natural or organic
  • Clichéd — relying on overused, predictable ideas

"Hokey" is a bit more all-purpose than these — it can mean any combination of fake, sentimental, cheap, and clichéd, all at once.

• It doesn't mean evil or immoral. It's about quality and authenticity, not ethics.
  • It doesn't mean boring. Hokey things can be lively and fun.
  • It doesn't mean stupid in a harsh sense — it's gentler than that.
  • It's not the same as wrong. Something can be factually correct and still be hokey (a hokey inspirational speech can contain true advice).

If you had to summarize: hokey = trying to be real, deep, or impressive, but coming across as fake, cheap, or embarrassingly simple instead. The person or thing behind it usually meant well — it just didn't have the craft, originality, or subtlety to pull it off convincingly. And depending on your mood, that can make you cringe, smile, or both.
7702: Hold means to keep something in place — to prevent it from falling, escaping, changing, or going away. This one idea runs through almost every use of the word. Once you grasp this, all its meanings will feel natural and connected.
1. To Grip or Carry Something Physically

The most direct meaning: to have something in your hands, arms, or body — keeping it secure.

  • She held the baby carefully.
  • He held the rope with both hands.
  • Hold this bag for a moment, please.

The key idea here is contact plus control. You're not just touching something — you are actively keeping it from slipping or falling.
2. To Contain Something

When a container "holds" something, it means the space inside it is keeping that thing. The container is doing the "gripping," in a way.

  • This bottle holds one litre of water.
  • The stadium holds 60,000 people.
  • My bag can't hold any more books.

Notice that here, "hold" is about capacity — how much something can keep inside itself.
3. To Support Weight

When something holds your weight, it means it is strong enough to keep you from falling — it is bearing you up.

  • Do you think this branch will hold me?
  • The old bridge couldn't hold the heavy truck.
  • The glue didn't hold — the shelf fell.

Here, "hold" is about not breaking or giving way under pressure.
4. To Keep Something in a Particular State or Position

You can hold something in a specific condition, meaning you keep it that way — you don't let it change.

  • Hold the door open for her.
  • Can you hold your arm still?
  • The soldiers held their position and didn't move back.
  • Hold your breath. (keep the air inside — don't exhale)

This is one of the most versatile uses. You are essentially freezing something in a state — stopping it from changing.
5. To Restrain or Stop Someone/Something

To hold someone (or something) means to stop them from moving forward, escaping, or going out of control.

  • The police officer held the man until help arrived.
  • She held back her tears. (she stopped herself from crying)
  • Nothing could hold back the flood.
  • Hold your horses! (an idiom meaning: slow down, wait, don't rush)

Here, the force of "hold" is resistance — actively blocking or preventing something.
6. To Have or Possess (a Position, Title, or Record)

When a person "holds" a title, job, or record, it means they currently have it — and they are keeping it.

  • She holds the world record for the 100m sprint.
  • He has held the position of manager for five years.
  • The party holds a majority in parliament.

Think of it this way: a title or record is like an object — and the person is gripping it, keeping it from passing to someone else.
7. To Organize or Conduct an Event

When people "hold" a meeting, election, or ceremony, they are making it happen — bringing it into existence and keeping it going.

  • The company will hold a meeting next Friday.
  • The country will hold elections in December.
  • They held a small ceremony to celebrate.

This might seem different, but the same idea is there: you are "keeping" the event in place — creating the space and time for it to happen.
8. To Believe or Consider Something True

When someone "holds" a view or belief, it means they have that belief in their mind and are keeping it — they stand by it.

  • She holds the belief that all people are equal.
  • The court held that the contract was invalid. (the court officially decided and stated this)
  • He holds his teacher in great respect. (he considers her worthy of deep respect)

Here, "hold" is about commitment to an idea or judgment. The mind is "gripping" a thought.
9. To Remain Valid or True

When a rule, theory, or promise "holds," it means it is still true, still working, still standing up.

  • Does this rule still hold in today's world?
  • The old agreement still holds.
  • The theory holds even under new evidence.

The opposite would be that something "doesn't hold" — meaning it has broken down, failed, or is no longer true.
10. To Wait (Especially on the Phone)

"Hold" commonly means to pause and wait — usually on a telephone line.

  • Please hold while I connect your call.
  • I've been on hold for twenty minutes. (waiting on the phone)

The idea is that you are being "kept in place" — you are waiting, suspended, until the other person comes back.
11. To Capture and Keep Attention

When something "holds" your attention or interest, it keeps you focused — it grips your mind and doesn't let go.

  • The book held my attention from the first page.
  • The speaker held the audience completely.
  • The film couldn't hold my interest past the first hour.
12. To Hold Someone Responsible or Accountable

This means to assign blame, duty, or liability to someone — to say "you are the one answerable for this."

  • I will hold you personally responsible for this mistake.
  • The company was held liable for the damage.
  • She held him accountable for what went wrong.
13. To Keep Something Reserved or Delayed for Someone

You can hold something for a person — meaning you set it aside and keep it until they arrive or are ready.

  • Can you hold a table for me? I'll arrive at 7.
  • The hotel held the room even though we were late.
  • Hold my order — I need to change something.
14. "Hold" in Music or Speech

To hold a note means to sing or play it continuously without stopping — to sustain it.

  • She held the final note for a full ten seconds.
  • Hold that sound a little longer.
Common Phrases and Their Meanings

These are very frequently used, so understanding them will help you greatly.

Hold on

  1. Wait. Hold on, I'll be right back.
  2. Grip tightly. Hold on to the railing — the stairs are steep.
  3. Endure through difficulty. Things are hard, but hold on a little longer.

Hold up

  1. To delay something or someone. Sorry I'm late — I got held up in traffic.
  2. To remain strong or valid. His argument doesn't hold up under examination.
  3. To rob someone, especially at gunpoint. The bank was held up this morning.
  4. To raise something. He held up his hand to ask a question.

Hold back

  1. To stop from moving forward. The crowd was held back by the barriers.
  2. To stop yourself from doing or saying something. She held back a laugh.
  3. To not share or give fully. Stop holding back — tell me the whole truth.

Hold out

  1. To extend something toward someone. He held out his hand to greet her.
  2. To last or survive. How long can the supplies hold out?
  3. To resist giving in. The workers held out for better pay.

Hold off

  1. To delay doing something. Hold off on sending the email — I need to check it.
  2. To keep something away. Can the team hold off their opponents?

Hold down

  1. To keep something pressed down. Hold down the button for three seconds.
  2. To keep a job. He finds it hard to hold down a steady job.

Hold against
To blame or resent someone for something, often unfairly.
I hope you won't hold my mistake against me.

Hold over

  1. To extend or continue something beyond its planned end. The film was so popular it was held over for another week.
  2. To use something as a threat. She held the secret over him to get what she wanted.

Hold together

  1. To remain in one piece. The old car is barely holding together.
  2. To keep a group united. She was the one who held the family together during the difficult times.

Hold your own
To perform well or at least not lose ground, especially in a difficult situation.
He's new to the game, but he can hold his own.

Hold your tongue
To stay silent; to not say something even though you want to.
I wanted to argue but I held my tongue.

Hold the line

  1. To stay on the phone and wait. Please hold the line.
  2. To not give in; to maintain a position. The government must hold the line on spending.
The Single Thread Running Through Everything

Even though "hold" has many uses, you will notice the same pulse in each one:

Hold = to keep something from changing, escaping, falling, or disappearing.

Whether you are holding a cup, holding a belief, holding a meeting, holding a record, or holding your breath — you are always keeping something in a particular place, state, or condition. That is the soul of this word.
7703:
To "hold at bay" means to keep something dangerous, threatening, or unwanted at a safe distance so that it cannot reach you, harm you, or get worse.

It does NOT mean to completely destroy or eliminate the threat. It means you are actively preventing it from getting closer or causing damage — but it is still there, and still requires your effort to keep it away.

Think of it like this: imagine holding a growling dog at arm's length. You have not defeated the dog. You have not made it disappear. But your effort is keeping it from biting you. That is "holding it at bay."
Where Did This Phrase Come From?

This idiom has a fascinating history rooted in medieval hunting.

The word "bay" comes from the Old French word "abai," which literally meant the barking sound of a dog. In old hunting practices, when a group of hunting hounds chased a wild animal (like a deer or a boar) and cornered it against a wall or in a tight space, the animal could no longer run. It would turn around and face the dogs. At this point, there was a standoff — the animal was trapped, but the dogs could not easily attack it either because the animal was defending itself. The dogs would surround it, barking loudly. This situation — where the cornered animal faces its pursuers and neither side can make a move — was called being "at bay."

So "at bay" originally meant this exact standoff: a dangerous creature is close, it is threatening, but something is keeping it from advancing further.

Over time, people started using this phrase far beyond hunting. If you can hold a threat "at bay," you are putting it in that same situation — present, dangerous, but held in place by your effort.
The Core Idea You Must Remember

The most important thing to understand about this idiom is its two-part nature:

  1. The threat is REAL and PRESENT. It has not gone away.
  2. Your effort is ACTIVELY preventing it from advancing. The moment you stop, the threat can move in.

This is why the phrase often implies ongoing struggle and vigilance. You are not relaxed. You are working hard to maintain that safe distance. It is like treading water — the moment you stop moving, you sink.

The structure is almost always:

[Someone] holds/held [something threatening] at bay
or
[Something threatening] is held at bay by [someone/something]

It can be used in three broad contexts:

1. Physical or Military Threats

When soldiers, guards, or people physically prevent an enemy, attacker, or danger from advancing.

The small group of soldiers held the enemy troops at bay until reinforcements arrived.

The firefighters held the spreading wildfire at bay by creating water barriers around the village.

2. Illness, Pain, or Physical Conditions

When medicine, treatment, or lifestyle keeps a sickness or pain from getting worse.

The medication is helping to hold the infection at bay, but the doctors say it is not cured yet.

She takes painkillers every few hours to hold the headache at bay.

3. Emotions, Problems, or Abstract Threats

When a person mentally or practically prevents a fear, worry, problem, or bad situation from overwhelming them.

He kept himself busy with work to hold his loneliness at bay.

The government introduced new policies to hold rising inflation at bay.

She took deep breaths to hold her anxiety at bay before the big speech.

You will often see "keep at bay" used instead of "hold at bay." These two phrases mean exactly the same thing and can be used interchangeably. Neither one is more correct than the other.

She kept her fears at bay. ✅
She held her fears at bay. ✅

Both are perfectly natural English.
What "Hold at Bay" Does NOT Mean

It is important to understand what this phrase does not mean, so you do not confuse it with similar phrases.

  • It does not mean to completely defeat or eliminate something. (That would be "wipe out," "eliminate," or "overcome.")
  • It does not mean to ignore or pretend a problem doesn't exist. (That would be "turn a blind eye" or "brush under the carpet.")
  • It does not mean to store or delay something comfortably. (That would be "put on hold" or "postpone.")

"Hold at bay" always involves a real, active threat that requires real, active effort to prevent.

Understanding expressions that are close in meaning helps you see this idiom more clearly:

  • "Fend off" — to push away or deflect a threat. (She fended off his questions skillfully.)
  • "Ward off" — to prevent something bad from affecting you. (Garlic is said to ward off illness.)
  • "Stave off" — to delay or prevent something negative, often temporarily. (They staved off bankruptcy with a last-minute deal.)
  • "Keep in check" — to control something so it does not get out of control. (Exercise helps keep stress in check.)
  • "Hold back" — to prevent something from moving forward. (He could not hold back his tears.)

All of these are similar in spirit to "hold at bay," but "hold at bay" carries the strongest sense of an active, ongoing struggle against something genuinely threatening.

Picture a knight in a castle, torch in hand, holding back a pack of wolves at the gate. He hasn't killed the wolves. He hasn't scared them away permanently. But as long as he stands there, waving that torch, the wolves cannot get through.

That is "holding at bay" in one image.
"Hold at bay" = to use continuous effort to keep a real threat, danger, or problem at a safe distance, preventing it from reaching you or getting worse — even though it is still present.
7704:
To truly understand this idiom, you need to start at its roots — because like most great idioms, its meaning is locked inside a real historical image.

Centuries ago, a king or queen would literally "hold court." This meant the monarch would sit on their throne in a grand hall, and people — nobles, advisors, visitors, ambassadors — would gather around them. Everyone came to the ruler. Everyone listened to the ruler. The monarch was the undisputed center of the room. They spoke, they judged, they entertained, they commanded attention. The people around them were an audience, not equals.

This is the scene the idiom is built on. Keep this image in your mind, because it makes everything else easy.
What It Means Today (The Idiomatic Meaning)

When we say someone "holds court" today, we mean:

A person becomes the dominant center of attention in a social situation, talking confidently and entertainingly while a group of people gather around them, listen to them, and give them their full focus.

The person "holding court" is behaving like that king or queen — not because they have a crown, but because of their personality, charm, confidence, humor, or authority. They own the room. People are drawn to them. Everyone else becomes the audience.
Breaking It Down — The Key Elements

For someone to truly be "holding court," a few things are usually happening at once:

1. They are talking. The person is usually speaking — telling stories, sharing opinions, cracking jokes, or giving advice. It's not a two-way conversation. It's more of a performance.

2. A group is gathered around them. One person talking to one other person is just a conversation. "Holding court" requires an audience — multiple people paying attention to the one person at the center.

3. The attention is on them — and they enjoy it. The person holding court is comfortable being the focal point. They're not shy about it. They thrive in that position, just like a monarch on their throne.

4. The tone is usually commanding or magnetic. The person isn't begging for attention. The attention comes naturally, because of who they are or how they carry themselves.
Tone and Connotation — Is It Positive or Negative?

This is one of the most important things to understand about this idiom: it can swing both ways depending on context and tone.

Positive / Admiring use:
When used admiringly, it suggests someone is charismatic, entertaining, socially confident, and captivating. You'd use it to describe someone who lights up a room.

"At the dinner party, my grandfather was holding court in the living room, keeping everyone in stitches with his old travel stories."

Here, the image is warm and flattering. He's beloved, funny, and magnetic.

Negative / Critical use:
When used with a hint of sarcasm or criticism, it can suggest someone who is arrogant, self-important, domineering, or monopolizing the conversation. They think they're royalty — but maybe others find them a bit much.

"He spent the whole evening holding court, talking about himself without asking a single question to anyone else."

Here, the image is unflattering. He's self-centered and tiresome.

The key is context. The words around the idiom — and the tone of voice — tell you which way it's being used.

Here are several examples across different settings so you can see how naturally it fits into everyday language:

  • "The famous author was holding court at the bookstore signing, surrounded by fans hanging on her every word."
  • "My uncle always holds court at family reunions. Everyone gathers around him to hear his jokes."
  • "The CEO walked into the conference room and immediately began holding court, dominating the entire meeting."
  • "She was holding court at the corner table, three colleagues leaning in, laughing at everything she said."
  • "He loves holding court at parties — the man just cannot stop talking about his opinions on everything."

Notice how in each case, one person is at the center, a group is around them, and all attention flows toward that person.

In real life, you'll often hear this phrase used to describe:

  • A charming storyteller at a social gathering
  • A charismatic leader or executive in a meeting
  • A celebrity or famous person surrounded by fans or admirers
  • A witty, talkative person who naturally becomes the life of the party
  • Occasionally, a self-important person who makes everything about themselves

It's equally important to know what this idiom does not mean, to avoid confusion:

  • It does not mean someone is literally in a court of law (though a judge commanding a courtroom comes close in spirit).
  • It does not apply to a quiet, shy person sitting alone.
  • It does not require someone to be famous or important — an ordinary person with a big personality can hold court at any gathering.
  • It is not about physical strength or power — it's entirely about social dominance and magnetic presence.

If you ever need to recall this idiom quickly, remember:

"Hold court" = to be the star of the show in a social situation, with people gathered around you, hanging on your every word — just like a king or queen on their throne.
One Final Tip for Using It

Use this idiom when you want to paint a vivid picture of someone commanding a room through sheer personality. It's a slightly elevated, expressive phrase — not overly formal, not too casual. It fits perfectly in storytelling, writing, journalism, and everyday conversation. When you say someone was "holding court," your listener immediately sees the scene: the crowd, the center, the performance. That visual power is exactly what makes this idiom so useful and enduring.
7705: "Hold down" is a phrasal verb — a verb combined with a small word (here, "down") that together create a meaning different from what each word means alone. "Hold" means to grip or keep, and "down" suggests a downward direction or staying in place. Together, they create several related but distinct meanings depending on the context.

1. To physically press or keep something in place

This is the most literal meaning. You use force to stop something from moving, lifting, or blowing away.

"Hold down the corner of the paper while I tape it."
"She had to hold down her hat in the strong wind."

Think of it as: your hand or body is keeping something stuck in its place.

2. To keep a job (very common usage)

When someone "holds down a job," it means they are able to keep that job steadily over time — especially when it requires effort or when the person faces difficulties.

"Despite his health problems, he managed to hold down a full-time job."
"She holds down two jobs to support her family."

The word "down" here gives a sense of stability — anchoring yourself to something. You are not letting the job slip away.

3. To suppress or prevent something from rising

Here, "hold down" means to keep something from increasing or getting out of control. It is often used with prices, costs, or numbers.

"The company is trying to hold down expenses this year."
"The government took steps to hold down inflation."

Think of it as pressing a lid down on a pot to stop things from bubbling over.

4. To physically restrain a person

This means to pin someone down with force so they cannot move. It is often used to describe a physical struggle or a medical situation.

"It took three people to hold down the patient during the procedure."
"The guards held him down until the police arrived."

5. To keep food or drink in your stomach

When you are sick and vomiting, or feeling nauseous, doctors might ask if you can "hold down" food or water. It means to eat or drink something without throwing it back up.

"She had such a bad stomach flu that she couldn't hold down any food."
"Try holding down small sips of water before eating anything solid."

6. To oppress or prevent someone from advancing

This is a figurative meaning. It means to keep a person (or a group of people) from progressing, succeeding, or being free — usually through unfair systems, power, or control.

"Many felt that the old laws were designed to hold poor communities down."
"He believed that his lack of education was holding him down."

Here, "down" is symbolic — like a weight placed on someone's shoulders, preventing them from rising.

7. Slang: To manage things / represent / stay loyal

In informal speech — especially in American slang and hip-hop culture — "hold it down" or "hold something down" means to take care of things responsibly, keep things running, or stay loyal to a person or a place while they are absent or in need.

"I'll be traveling for two weeks. Can you hold it down at the office?"
"He always held it down for his neighborhood."

You can think of it as: being a reliable anchor. You keep things from falling apart. You represent something or someone with pride and loyalty.

All these meanings share a single underlying idea: preventing something from moving upward, escaping, increasing, or falling apart. Whether it is a physical object, a job, a price, a person, or a situation — "hold down" is always about maintaining control, stability, or suppression.

• "Hold down" can take an object between the two words or after them:
    "Hold the paper down" ✅
    "Hold down the paper" ✅
    "Hold it down" ✅
  • With a pronoun (it, him, her, them), the pronoun almost always goes between "hold" and "down":
    "Hold it down" ✅
    "Hold down it" ❌ — this sounds unnatural.

Physical object → pressing it to keep it still
Employment → keeping a job steadily
Prices or levels → preventing an increase
A person (physical) → restraining with force
Food/drink → keeping it in the stomach after eating
A person (social) → oppressing or blocking progress
Slang → managing things / being loyal / representing

Once you understand that "hold down" is fundamentally about keeping something stable, controlled, or suppressed, every use of it will start to feel natural and make immediate sense to you.
7706:
To hold forth means to talk at length about a topic, usually in a confident, opinionated, and often self-important way.

When someone "holds forth," they are not having a normal back-and-forth conversation. They are doing most — or all — of the talking. Think of it as one person turning into a speaker while everyone else becomes an audience, whether they wanted to be one or not.

This is where the phrase gets interesting.

"Hold forth" almost always carries a slightly critical or ironic tone. It quietly suggests that:

  • The speaker is going on too long.
  • The speaker is in love with the sound of their own voice.
  • The speaker is being a bit preachy or self-important.
  • The listeners may be bored, trapped, or politely enduring the speech.

The speaker, however, usually doesn't notice or doesn't care. They are thoroughly enjoying themselves.

That said, it is not always harshly negative. Sometimes it is used with mild affection — like when someone passionately talks about a topic they love, even if they go on a bit too long. The tone depends heavily on context.

A good way to feel the word: imagine being stuck at a dinner table next to someone who will not stop explaining their views on something. That person is "holding forth."
The Grammar: How to Use It

"Hold forth" is a phrasal verb — a verb made up of two words that work together as a single unit.

Structure:

[Subject] + hold forth + on/about + [topic]

The prepositions you use after it are "on" or "about."

  • "He held forth on the importance of diet."
  • "She held forth about the flaws in the government."

You can also use it without mentioning the topic if the topic is already clear from context:

  • "He held forth for a full hour." (We understand he was talking about something.)

Important note: "Hold forth" is intransitive, meaning it does not take a direct object. You do not "hold forth an idea." You simply "hold forth" — and then optionally name the topic using "on" or "about."

Here are examples across different situations so you can see it in action:

  1. At a dinner party:

"My uncle held forth on the failures of modern education for the entire meal. Nobody could get a word in."

  1. In a workplace:

"The manager held forth about productivity strategies in a meeting that was supposed to last 20 minutes but went on for two hours."

  1. Used affectionately:

"She held forth about her favorite novels with such passion that we actually enjoyed listening."

  1. In formal writing:

"The politician held forth on immigration policy to an increasingly restless crowd."

  1. Without naming the topic:

"He found an audience and held forth for the rest of the evening."

The word "forth" in older English meant "forward" or "outward" — as in pushing something out toward others. Think of phrases like "come forth," "put forth," or "go forth."

So "hold forth" originally carried the image of extending or putting forward your words and opinions — reaching them out toward your listeners. It was like physically offering your views to the room.

Over time, this evolved to specifically describe speaking at length in an opinionated, extended way — with the gradual implication that perhaps the speaker is offering a bit too much of their views for a bit too long.
How It Differs From Similar Words

There are several words and phrases that feel similar to "hold forth," but they are not the same:

Lecture — To lecture someone implies a formal or educational setting, OR it means to scold someone. It doesn't carry quite the same image of someone enjoying themselves at a social gathering.

Pontificate — This is even stronger and more negative than "hold forth." To pontificate means to speak in a very pompous, arrogant way, as if you are the ultimate authority. "Hold forth" can be gentler.

Ramble — To ramble means to talk without direction, jumping from topic to topic without focus. "Hold forth" is different because the person does have a focus — they are usually confidently sticking to their topic.

Go on and on — This is a casual, informal way to describe the same behavior. "Hold forth" is slightly more formal and more literary.

Hold court — This is a close cousin. When someone "holds court," people are willingly gathered around them, often admiring what they're saying. It has a more positive feel. "Hold forth" doesn't require a willing or admiring audience.

Think of a king or queen on a throne, holding out their hand, demanding everyone listen while they speak forth — on and on — about their royal opinions. No one leaves. No one interrupts. The king just keeps going.

That image — one person commanding attention, speaking at length, and clearly enjoying it — is the heart of "hold forth."

QuestionAnswer
  • What does it mean? To talk at great length about something in a confident, often self-important way.
  • What's the tone? Mildly critical or ironic, sometimes affectionate.
  • Who is "holding forth"? Someone who talks a lot, mostly to themselves — the audience is secondary.
  • What prepositions follow it? "On" or "about."
  • Is it formal or casual? Slightly formal/literary, but understood in everyday speech.

Once you start noticing this phrase, you'll see it everywhere — in novels, journalism, and conversation. And the next time you're trapped at a party while someone explains their opinions on something for the fourth time that evening, you'll know exactly what to call it.
7707: "Hold off" is a phrasal verb — a verb ("hold") combined with a particle ("off") to create a meaning that is different from either word alone. It has two main, distinct meanings in everyday English, plus a special use with weather.
Meaning 1: To Delay or Postpone Something

This is the most common meaning. When you "hold off" doing something, you deliberately wait before doing it. You have the ability to act, but you choose — or are asked — to pause.

Think of it like pressing a pause button on an action.

"Can you hold off sending that email? I want to read it first."
"Let's hold off on making a decision until we hear back from them."
"The company held off launching the product until they fixed the bugs."
"Hold off a little longer — he's almost here."

There is usually a reason behind the waiting: caution, uncertainty, or the need for better timing. The choice to wait is conscious and deliberate.

Common patterns you'll see with this meaning:

"Hold off on + noun" → "Hold off on the announcement."
"Hold off + verb-ing" → "Hold off making any promises."
"Hold off until + time" → "Hold off until Friday."
"Hold off for + duration" → "Hold off for a few more days."

Note that "hold off" in this meaning is often used without a direct object — you simply say "let's hold off" or "we held off," and the context makes clear what is being delayed.
Meaning 2: To Resist, Fight Off, or Keep Someone Away

This meaning is about successfully preventing someone or something from reaching you, defeating you, or overcoming you. You are under pressure — from a competitor, an opponent, a crowd, an attack — and you manage to stop them.

Picture a goalkeeper in the last five minutes of a football match desperately defending the goal. They are "holding off" the attacking team.

"The small army held off the invaders for three weeks."
"She held off her rivals to win the championship."
"Despite being exhausted, the boxer held off his opponent until the final bell."
"The security team held off the crowd until the police arrived."

This meaning is very common in sports, competition, military contexts, and any situation where one side is under pressure and resisting the other.

This is a special, fixed use where bad weather — usually rain or snow — is the subject. When weather "holds off," it means it hasn't arrived yet; it is staying away.

Notice that in this case, nobody is doing the holding. The weather itself is described as "holding off," meaning it is delaying its own arrival.

"I hope the rain holds off until after our picnic."
"The snow held off all weekend, so the roads were clear."
"If the storm holds off until tonight, we can finish the match."

This use is only for weather. You would not say "the meeting held off" using this same structure — that would revert to Meaning 1, which needs a human subject.
Grammar: How to Place the Object

"Hold off" is a separable phrasal verb in Meaning 2. This means the noun object can go either after "off" or between "hold" and "off":

"The soldiers held off the attackers." ✅
"The soldiers held the attackers off." ✅

Both are correct. However, when the object is a pronoun (him, her, them, it, us), it must go between "hold" and "off":

"Hold them off." ✅
"Hold off them." ❌

This is a firm rule in English with separable phrasal verbs: pronouns always go in the middle.

For Meaning 1, this separation does not typically apply, because the structure uses "on" or a gerund (-ing form) rather than a direct noun object placed after "off."

Knowing how the verb changes across tenses helps you use it naturally:

Present: "We hold off / She holds off"
Past: "We held off / She held off"
Present participle (ongoing): "We are holding off / She is holding off"
Past participle: "We have held off"

"Hold off" sits in the neutral-to-informal range. You can use it comfortably in everyday conversation, professional emails, news writing, and fiction. It is not slang, but it is not stiff or formal either. It is a natural, all-purpose phrase.

Several phrases are close in meaning. Understanding the fine differences between them will sharpen your English considerably.

Hold off vs. Put off: For Meaning 1 (delay), these are nearly interchangeable. "Put off the meeting until Monday" and "hold off on the meeting until Monday" are both natural. The difference is that "put off" can also mean to disgust or repel someone ("His attitude put me off"), while "hold off" never carries that meaning.

Hold off vs. Hold back: "Hold back" often refers to restraining an emotion or stopping yourself from saying something impulsive. "She held back her tears." While "hold back" can also mean to delay, "hold off" sounds more natural and specific when postponing a concrete action or decision.

Hold off vs. Fend off: "Fend off" is a near-synonym for Meaning 2. However, "fend off" suggests more active, physical effort — like swatting something away. "Hold off" is broader and works equally well in sports, competition, and physical confrontation. You could say either "she fended off the attack" or "she held off the attack," but only "hold off" naturally extends to non-physical competition like a business rivalry.

Hold off vs. Hold out: "Hold out" means to endure or resist over a longer, sustained period, often against overwhelming odds. "The rebels held out for months." "Hold off" focuses more on a specific moment or episode of resistance, while "hold out" emphasizes stamina over time.

Hold off vs. Ward off: "Ward off" means to prevent something harmful from affecting you — illness, bad luck, danger. "She drank ginger tea to ward off a cold." "Hold off" can be used similarly in the context of physical opponents or attacks, but "ward off" is more limited to keeping harm away from oneself personally.
A Core Idea That Ties Both Meanings Together

Think of the word "off" as meaning "away from." In both main meanings of "hold off," you are keeping something away:

In Meaning 1, you are keeping an action away from the present moment — you are not letting it happen yet.

In Meaning 2, you are keeping a person, force, or opponent away from reaching or overcoming you.

The weather use follows the same logic: the rain is keeping itself away.

All three uses share the same underlying concept — distance and delay. Something is being kept from arriving, happening, or succeeding, at least for now.

"Hold off" means one of three things:

To delay something: "Hold off on the decision until tomorrow."
To resist someone or something: "They held off the attacking team until the final whistle."
For weather to stay away: "I hope the rain holds off."

With pronouns in Meaning 2, always place the pronoun in the middle: "hold them off," never "hold off them."

That is everything you need to know about "hold off" — its meanings, its grammar, its register, its related phrases, and the logic behind it.
7708:
To hold one's ground means to refuse to change your position, opinion, or decision when someone is pressuring you to do so. It means you stay firm and strong, even when things get tough or someone is pushing back against you.

Think of it this way: if someone is trying to move you — physically or with arguments — and you simply don't budge, you are holding your ground.
Where It Comes From (Origin)

This idiom comes from real, physical warfare. In old battles, soldiers were given a piece of land (ground) to defend. Their job was to not let the enemy push them off that spot. If they stood firm and didn't retreat, they were "holding their ground."

Over centuries, this military image moved into everyday language. People started using it not just for soldiers, but for any situation where someone refuses to back down — in arguments, negotiations, or personal decisions.
Literal vs. Figurative Meaning

Literally, it means staying in a physical position without moving backward. A soldier holds his ground on a battlefield.

Figuratively (which is how it is almost always used today), it means staying firm in your opinion, belief, decision, or stance without letting others change it through pressure, criticism, or intimidation.
Simple Breakdown

Imagine you believe something strongly. A friend argues with you and tries to convince you that you're wrong. You listen, but you still think you're right — so you don't change your mind. You held your ground.

Or imagine your boss asks you to do something that goes against your values. You politely but firmly say no, even though your boss keeps pushing. You held your ground.

The core idea is always the same: pressure comes at you, but you don't move.
Real-Life Examples

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how flexible this idiom is:

In a debate or argument:
"Everyone in the room disagreed with her, but she held her ground and explained her reasoning calmly."

In a negotiation:
"The buyer kept asking for a lower price, but the seller held his ground and refused to go below the original amount."

In a personal/social situation:
"His friends were pressuring him to skip the exam and go to the party, but he held his ground and stayed home to study."

In a physical or sports context (closer to the literal meaning):
"The goalkeeper held his ground even as the striker charged toward him."
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom almost always carries a positive or admirable tone. When we say someone "held their ground," we usually mean it as a compliment — it suggests that person showed courage, confidence, and self-belief.

It implies:

  • The person faced real pressure or opposition.
  • Giving in would have been the easier path.
  • They chose not to give in, which takes strength.

However, it can sometimes be used in a neutral or slightly negative way — for example, if someone holds their ground on a bad idea, refusing to listen to good advice. In that case, it edges closer to being stubborn. Context decides the tone.
The Difference Between "Holding Your Ground" and Being Stubborn

This is a subtle but important difference.

Holding your ground suggests you have good reason to stay firm — your position is valid, and the pressure on you is unfair or wrong. There is dignity in it.

Being stubborn suggests you refuse to change even when the other person has a better point and you're simply being unreasonable.

The action may look the same from the outside, but the justification is what separates the two. A person who holds their ground is respected; a person who is merely stubborn is seen as difficult.
Common Variations of This Idiom

The idiom appears in a few slightly different forms, all meaning the same thing:

  • "Hold your ground" — the most common form, often used as advice or instruction. (Don't let them bully you — hold your ground.)
  • "Held his/her/their ground" — used to describe what someone did in the past.
  • "Holding my ground" — used when speaking about yourself in the present moment. (I'm not backing down; I'm holding my ground.)
  • "Stand one's ground" — a very close cousin of this idiom, almost interchangeable. It means exactly the same thing.
Similar Idioms (Same Idea)

These idioms carry a very similar meaning and are good to know alongside this one:

  • "Stand one's ground" — the most direct synonym.
  • "Stick to your guns" — refuse to change your opinion even under pressure.
  • "Not back down" — straightforwardly refuse to retreat from a position.
  • "Stand firm" — remain fixed and strong in a decision or belief.
Opposite Idioms (Opposite Idea)

These mean the opposite — giving in to pressure:

  • "Back down" — to withdraw from a position under pressure.
  • "Cave in" — to give up and agree with the other side.
  • "Give ground" — to surrender a little, to allow the other side to gain.
  • "Throw in the towel" — to give up completely.
When Should You Use This Idiom?

You can use it in both spoken and written English. It is perfectly appropriate in:

  • Everyday conversations
  • Professional and business settings
  • Essays and articles
  • Storytelling and news reports

It is not slang — it is a well-established, respected idiom that sounds natural in formal and informal situations alike.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"Hold one's ground" = stay firm in your position and don't let pressure, criticism, or opposition make you back down.

Picture a soldier who refuses to move from his spot no matter how fierce the attack — that image will always bring this idiom back to you.
7709:
To "hold one's own" means to perform competently or survive successfully in a difficult or competitive situation, without being defeated, overwhelmed, or outshone — even when the odds are not in your favor.

Think of it this way: imagine you are in a tug-of-war. You may not be winning, but you are not losing either. You are keeping your position. You are not being dragged forward. That is holding your own.

It does not mean you are dominating or winning. It simply means you are standing firm, keeping up, and not falling behind — which, depending on the situation, can be an impressive achievement.

• "Hold" = to maintain, to keep, to not let go of
  • "Own" = what belongs to you — your position, your place, your ground

So literally, the phrase means "to keep what is yours." Over time, it evolved into a figurative expression meaning to maintain your standing or performance in a challenging situation.

This idiom carries a tone of quiet strength and resilience. It is usually said with respect or admiration, because the person "holding their own" is often in a tough spot — competing against stronger people, facing a hard challenge, or dealing with pressure — and yet they are not crumbling.

It acknowledges difficulty honestly. It does not pretend the person is thriving. But it says: "They are not giving up, and they are not being beaten."
Where and How It Is Used

This idiom is very versatile. It is used in everyday conversation, writing, sports commentary, business, and more. Here are the main contexts where you'll encounter it:

1. In competition or performance
When someone competes against people who are more experienced or skilled, and they manage to keep up without embarrassing themselves.

"She was the youngest player in the chess tournament, but she held her own against players twice her age."

2. In arguments or debates
When someone is challenged, questioned, or pressured intellectually, and they defend their position well without being talked over or pushed around.

"The journalist held his own during the intense interview, answering every tough question confidently."

3. In difficult or unfamiliar situations
When someone is thrown into a challenging environment but manages to cope and function adequately.

"It was his first week as a chef, but he held his own during the busy dinner rush."

4. In health or physical endurance
When someone is ill, injured, or physically challenged but is not getting worse — they are maintaining their condition.

"The patient had a rough night, but by morning the doctors said she was holding her own."

5. In social situations
When someone is in a group of people who are more knowledgeable, powerful, or experienced, and they still manage to participate meaningfully without being ignored or embarrassed.

"He was nervous about joining the senior team meeting, but he held his own and even made a great point."

✦ It implies a challenge exists.
You would not say someone is "holding their own" if the situation is easy. The phrase only makes sense when there is pressure, difficulty, or competition. If you say someone "held their own," the listener automatically understands: "The situation was tough."

✦ It is praise, but modest praise.
It is not the same as saying someone excelled or won. It is a genuine compliment that says: "Given the difficulty of the situation, they performed admirably." Think of it as saying, "They did not fail when failing was easy."

✦ It can be used for yourself too.
People sometimes say it in the first person to express that they survived or coped well in a tough situation.

"I wasn't sure I could keep up with the conversation, but I think I held my own."

✦ The verb form is flexible.
You will see it as:

  • "hold your own" (present/future)
  • "held her own" (past)
  • "holding his own" (present continuous)
  • "holds their own" (simple present, general truth)

The phrase comes from the world of physical combat and military conflict, dating back to at least the 16th century. When soldiers or fighters were told to "hold their own," it meant: do not give up your ground, maintain your position on the battlefield. Losing ground literally meant defeat or death.

Over the centuries, as language evolved and became more figurative, this battlefield concept expanded into everyday life — and today it applies to any situation where you are under pressure and need to maintain your position, whether physically, mentally, or competitively.
How It Differs from Similar Expressions

"Hold one's own" vs. "hold one's ground"
These are close, but not identical. "Hold one's ground" emphasizes refusing to change your opinion or position — it is more about stubbornness or firm belief. "Hold one's own" is more about performance and capability in a challenging situation.

"Hold one's own" vs. "keep up"
"Keep up" simply means to match the pace of others. "Hold one's own" goes slightly deeper — it implies surviving or performing well even under pressure or disadvantage, not just matching pace.

"Hold one's own" vs. "hold one's head high"
"Hold one's head high" is about maintaining dignity and self-respect, often after failure or hardship. "Hold one's own" is about competent performance during a challenge, not just dignity after it.

Picture a soldier planting their feet firmly on a battlefield. Everyone around is being pushed back. But this soldier does not move. They hold their ground. They hold what is their own.

Now apply that image to any tough situation in life — a job interview, a debate, a sports match, a hard exam — and you have the feeling of "holding one's own" perfectly captured.

"Hold one's own" means to perform adequately and stand firm in a difficult or competitive situation, without being overwhelmed or defeated — even if you are not the strongest, most experienced, or most powerful person in the room.
7710:
To hold one's tongue means to stay silent on purpose, especially when you really want to say something but choose not to. It is about deliberate, conscious self-control over your speech.

The key word here is deliberate. You are not silent because you have nothing to say. You have something to say — maybe a lot — but you make an active decision to keep it to yourself. That effort, that internal struggle to stop words from coming out, is exactly what this idiom captures.
The Literal Picture Behind the Idiom

Idioms often come from a vivid physical image, and this one is no different.

Imagine actually using your fingers to grab and hold your tongue — the muscle inside your mouth. If you do that, you physically cannot speak. The idiom takes this literal image and uses it as a metaphor for silencing yourself mentally and emotionally. The mouth wants to speak. You stop it.

This is one of the reasons the idiom is so effective — the image is instantly understandable to anyone.
The History and Origin

This idiom is centuries old. It appears in early English translations of the Bible (for example, in the Book of Job and Psalms, where people are urged to restrain their speech). It also appears in the works of William Shakespeare and other writers from the 16th and 17th centuries.

For example, in Shakespeare's Othello, the phrase is used in a commanding tone to tell someone to stop talking.

The expression has been in continuous use in the English language for over 500 years, which tells you just how universal and timeless the idea of choosing silence is.
The Exact Feeling It Describes

This idiom carries a very specific emotional weight. It usually implies one or more of these feelings:

Frustration or anger — You are annoyed or upset, and you want to say something sharp or confrontational, but you stop yourself.

Wisdom or strategy — You realize that speaking right now would make things worse, so you wisely stay quiet.

Politeness or respect — You disagree or are offended, but out of respect for the situation or person, you choose not to speak.

Discipline — You are in a situation (a formal meeting, an argument with a superior, a tense family moment) where speaking would be inappropriate, so you hold back.

So when someone says they "held their tongue," you understand immediately that it cost them something. They wanted to speak. They didn't. That tension is built into the idiom.
How It Is Structured (The Grammar)

The idiom changes its pronoun depending on who is doing the holding. Here are all the forms you will encounter:

I held my tongue. (past tense — you stayed silent)
She held her tongue. (past tense — she stayed silent)
He held his tongue. (past tense — he stayed silent)
They held their tongues. (past tense — they stayed silent)
I am holding my tongue. (present — you are currently staying silent)
Hold your tongue! (command — telling someone to be quiet)
I had to hold my tongue. (past — you felt compelled to stay silent)

The phrase "hold one's tongue" is simply the standard dictionary form, where one's is a placeholder that gets replaced by my, your, his, her, their depending on the sentence.
Real-Life Example Sentences

These examples show the idiom in action across different situations:

At work:
"My manager said something completely wrong in the meeting, but I held my tongue because I didn't want to embarrass him in front of everyone."

In an argument:
"She was so rude to me, but I held my tongue and walked away before I said something I'd regret."

In a formal setting:
"During the ceremony, he had to hold his tongue even though he strongly disagreed with what was being said."

As a piece of advice:
"Sometimes it's wiser to hold your tongue than to win an argument and lose a friendship."

As a command (firm/old-fashioned):
"Hold your tongue! You are speaking out of turn."
The Two Ways the Idiom Is Used

There is a subtle but important difference in how this idiom gets used:

1. Describing your own restraint (most common)
Here, the person is reflecting on a choice they made to stay silent. It carries a tone of self-discipline and sometimes pride or sacrifice.
"I held my tongue even though I had every right to speak."

2. As a command to someone else (less common, quite strong)
When you say "Hold your tongue!" to another person, you are sharply telling them to stop talking. This usage sounds quite stern and even old-fashioned in modern English. You are more likely to hear it in literature, historical dramas, or from someone who is very formal or very angry. In everyday modern conversation, people would more likely say "Be quiet," "Zip it," or "Stop talking."
Similar Idioms (and the Small Differences)

Bite one's tongue
This is the closest cousin to "hold one's tongue." Both mean stopping yourself from speaking. However, "bite one's tongue" often has a stronger sense of physical struggle — as if the words are almost coming out and you are barely stopping them. It also sometimes implies you accidentally said something and then wish you hadn't.
"I nearly told her the truth, but I bit my tongue at the last second."

Keep one's mouth shut
This is more informal and blunter. It means the same thing — staying silent — but lacks the sense of emotional restraint. It can also be used as advice or a warning.
"Just keep your mouth shut and let them do the talking."

Zip one's lips
Very informal and casual. Often used with children or in light-hearted contexts.
"Zip your lips — this is a surprise party!"

Stay mum
"Mum" here means silent (not mother). "Staying mum" means keeping quiet, especially about a secret. It focuses more on secrecy than on self-control.
"She stayed mum about the plans."
Opposite Idioms (What It Means to NOT Hold Your Tongue)

Speak one's mind — To say exactly what you think, without holding back.
Shoot one's mouth off — To talk too much, often carelessly or without thinking.
Let it slip — To accidentally say something you were supposed to keep quiet.
Blurt out — To suddenly say something without thinking or intending to.

If someone does the opposite of holding their tongue, they usually say too much, say the wrong thing, or speak at the wrong moment.
Tone and Register — When Can You Use It?

This idiom is comfortably used in both formal and informal situations.

In formal writing (essays, books, journalism), it sounds natural and even elegant.
In casual conversation, it fits perfectly well.
In literature and historical texts, it appears very frequently.

It is not slang and is not considered rude or inappropriate in any context. It is a fully respectable, standard idiom of the English language.
The Deeper Wisdom Inside This Idiom

One reason this idiom has survived for 500+ years is that it points to something deeply human. We all know what it feels like to have words burning in our throat that we choose — or force ourselves — not to say.

The idiom quietly acknowledges that silence can be an act of strength, not weakness. The person who holds their tongue is not passive. They are exercising control. They are choosing peace over conflict, wisdom over reaction, or respect over the satisfaction of being heard.

This is why the idiom is so often used in a tone of pride or quiet dignity — "I held my tongue" — as if to say: I had every reason to speak. I chose not to. That took something from me, but I made the right call.
Quick Summary

Hold one's tongue = To deliberately stay silent when you want to speak, out of wisdom, politeness, self-control, or strategy. It implies effort and restraint, not passive silence. It has been used in English for over 500 years and remains perfectly natural in modern usage across both formal and informal contexts.
7711: "Hold out" is a phrasal verb — a combination of a verb (hold) and a particle (out) that together create a meaning that is often different from the individual words. It can also be used as a noun (a holdout). It has several distinct meanings, and you will encounter all of them in everyday English.
The Core Idea Behind "Hold Out"

Before diving into each meaning, here's a unifying idea that makes all the meanings easier to remember:

"Hold out" always involves some kind of resistance, extension, or continuation against a force or limit.

Whether you're physically extending your hand, resisting pressure, or hoping a supply lasts long enough — the idea of stretching, enduring, or refusing to give in is always present.
Meaning 1 — To Physically Extend Something Toward Someone

This is the most literal meaning. When you hold something out, you stretch or extend it in someone's direction, usually as an offer.

Think of it as: You are physically "putting something out" into the space between you and another person.

Examples:

  • She held out her hand for him to shake.
  • The child held out a flower to his mother.
  • The officer held out a badge to identify himself.

Important note: This meaning is almost always about a physical gesture. The thing being extended is literally moved outward.
Meaning 2 — To Resist, Survive, or Endure Despite Pressure or Difficulty

This is probably the most common and important meaning. When someone holds out, they keep going, keep resisting, or keep surviving even when things are very hard or when someone/something is pushing them to stop or give up.

Think of it as: You are "holding your position" against a force that wants to break or move you.

Examples:

  • The soldiers held out for two weeks before they finally surrendered.
  • Can you hold out a little longer? We're almost at the hospital.
  • She held out against the pressure from her boss and refused to quit.
  • The small company managed to hold out during the economic crisis.

Key signal: You'll often see "hold out" used with a time phrase (hold out for two days, hold out until help arrives) or against a difficulty (hold out against the enemy, hold out through the storm).
Meaning 3 — To Last Long Enough (of Supplies, Resources, or Conditions)

When a supply or resource holds out, it means it is sufficient and lasts as long as it is needed. This is different from Meaning 2 because here, a thing — not a person — is doing the "holding out." This meaning is also sometimes used for conditions like weather.

Think of it as: Will this thing stretch far enough to meet the need?

Examples:

  • I hope our food supplies hold out until the rescue team arrives.
  • Will the car's battery hold out for the whole journey?
  • The good weather held out all week, which was lucky for the hikers.

Key signal: The subject is usually a resource or condition (water, battery, fuel, weather, money), and there is often an implied deadline or goal ("until...", "for the whole...").
Meaning 4 — To Withhold Something From Someone ("Hold Out on Someone")

The phrase "hold out on someone" means to keep something secret or to refuse to give someone what they deserve or expect — information, money, a share of something, etc.

Think of it as: You're keeping something pulled back, not giving it out.

Examples:

  • I know you have more information — why are you holding out on me?
  • He sold the business and held out on his partner, keeping the extra profit for himself.
  • Are you holding out on us? Tell us what really happened!

Important: This meaning almost always uses the structure "hold out on [someone]." The emphasis is on unfairness or secrecy.
Meaning 5 — To Offer or Present the Possibility of Something (Especially Hope)

When something holds out hope, a promise, or a prospect, it means it presents or suggests that possibility. This is mostly used in formal or written English.

Think of it as: Something is "extending" the possibility to you — like an outstretched hand offering something abstract.

Examples:

  • The new medicine holds out hope for millions of patients worldwide.
  • The peace talks hold out the prospect of an end to the conflict.
  • Scientists hold out the possibility that life could exist on other planets.

Key signal: The subject is usually a situation, discovery, or development. The object is always something abstract like hope, promise, the prospect of, the possibility of.
Meaning 6 — To Refuse to Accept Less Than You Want (Hold Out For Something)

When someone holds out for something, they refuse to compromise or settle. They keep insisting on getting exactly what they want, even under pressure to accept less.

Think of it as: You are "holding your ground" until you get what you are demanding.

Examples:

  • The workers held out for a 15% pay raise and refused to go back to work.
  • She held out for a better job offer instead of taking the first one she received.
  • He held out for the exact price he wanted and eventually sold the house at full value.

Key signal: This meaning almost always uses the structure "hold out for [something]." It implies patience, stubbornness, or strong determination.
The Noun Form: "A Holdout"

When written as one word — holdout — it becomes a noun. It refers to a person or group that refuses to go along with others, refuses to accept a deal, or refuses to change their position.

Examples:

  • Everyone agreed to the contract except for one holdout.
  • He was the last holdout who refused to sell his house to the developer.
  • There were a few holdouts in the committee who kept blocking the vote.

A holdout is usually seen as someone stubborn, but depending on the context, it can be admirable (standing firm on a principle) or frustrating (blocking progress).
Grammar: Is "Hold Out" Separable?

Yes — for most meanings, "hold out" is a separable phrasal verb. This means you can place an object between "hold" and "out."

  • ✅ She held out her hand. → ✅ She held her hand out. (Both are correct.)
  • ✅ He held out the document. → ✅ He held the document out.

However, when you use a pronoun (he, she, it, them, etc.), you must put it in the middle:

  • ✅ She held it out. ← Correct
  • ❌ She held out it. ← Incorrect

For meanings that use a fixed structure like "hold out for" or "hold out on someone," separation does not apply — those are fixed phrases.
Quick Summary of All Meanings

MeaningCore IdeaStructure
1Physically extend somethingHold out + [object]
2Resist or survive difficultyHold out + [time/against]
3Supplies last long enough[Supply/resource] + holds out
4Withhold from someone unfairlyHold out on + [person]
5Present hope or a possibilityHold out + [hope/promise/prospect]
6Refuse to accept lessHold out for + [demand]
NounA person refusing to go alongA holdout
One Final Tip to Remember It All

The phrase "hold out" always carries the sense of something being stretched, extended, or maintained against a limit or pressure — whether that's a hand being extended, a soldier resisting an enemy, a water supply being stretched thin, information being kept back, or a negotiator refusing to budge. Once you feel that underlying thread, all the meanings click into place naturally.
7712:
"Hold out for" means to refuse to accept something until you get exactly what you want.

When you "hold out for" something, you are saying:

"No, I will not take what you are offering me right now. I will wait. I will be patient. I will only say yes when I get the specific thing I want."

So there are two key ideas working together here:

  1. You are being offered something, but you are refusing it.
  2. You are waiting specifically for something better — something particular that you have in your mind.
A Simple Picture to Understand It

Imagine you are selling your old bicycle. Someone offers you $50. You know it is worth $100. So you say, "No, thank you," and you keep waiting until someone pays you $100.

You are holding out for $100.

You are not giving up. You are not accepting less. You are standing firm and waiting for what you truly want.

The pattern is simple:

hold out for + [the thing you want]

Here are clean examples:

  • She is holding out for a better job offer.
  • He held out for more money.
  • Don't hold out for a perfect moment — it may never come.
  • They are holding out for a house with a garden.
  • I held out for the exact color I wanted and finally found it.

Notice that "hold out for" is always followed by a noun or noun phrase — the specific thing you are waiting or hoping to get.

This phrase carries three hidden ideas inside it that you must feel, not just know:

1. Refusal
You are actively saying no to what is being offered right now. This is not passive waiting. This is a deliberate choice to reject the current offer.

2. Patience and persistence
You are willing to wait — even if it takes a long time — because you believe what you want is worth waiting for.

3. Risk
This is the most important hidden idea. When you hold out for something, there is always a risk that you might end up with nothing at all. The offer you refused might not come back. The better deal might never arrive. This risk is almost always present in the background of this phrase. That's what makes holding out for something a bold or brave decision.
Real-Life Situations Where You'll Hear This Phrase

In a job or salary negotiation:

"The company offered her $70,000 a year, but she held out for $85,000 — and got it."

In buying or selling:

"He refused three offers on his house. He was holding out for the right buyer."

In sports (very common in professional sports):

"The player refused to sign the contract. He was holding out for a bigger deal."

In relationships:

"She's not dating anyone right now. She's holding out for someone who truly respects her."

In everyday decisions:

"I didn't buy any shoes on sale. I'm holding out for the exact pair I want."

When someone says, "I'm holding out for...", you should sense a person who:

  • Knows what they want
  • Is not desperate
  • Has self-belief
  • Is willing to be uncomfortable or wait rather than settle for less

The phrase is often used with admiration — as in, "Good for you for not settling." But it can also carry a warning — as in, "Don't hold out for too long, or you'll miss your chance."
"Hold Out For" vs. Words It's Confused With

"Wait for" — This just means you expect something to arrive. There's no refusal involved.

"I'm waiting for the bus." ← You didn't refuse the bus. You're simply expecting it.

"Hold out for" — You are actively refusing current options and staying firm until a specific thing comes.

"I'm holding out for a direct flight, even though cheaper connecting flights are available." ← You are saying no to the connecting flights.

"Settle for" — This is the opposite of "hold out for." When you settle for something, you accept something less than what you wanted because you got tired of waiting or felt you had no choice.

"I held out for months, but in the end I settled for a smaller apartment."

This phrase is neutral — it is perfectly natural in both casual conversation and professional settings.

  • ✅ You can say it to a friend: "Hold out for someone who treats you right."
  • ✅ You can say it in a business meeting: "We're holding out for a more favorable contract."
  • ✅ You can read it in a newspaper: "The union is holding out for a 10% wage increase."
A Memorable Way to Remember It

Think of the image of a person holding their hand out, palm up, refusing to close it around something being offered to them — waiting with an open hand until something better lands in it.

Holding out = not closing the deal. For = specifically waiting for this thing.
"Hold out for" means to patiently refuse to accept anything less than the specific thing you want, even if it means waiting a long time or taking a risk.
7713:
"Hold sway" means to have strong power, control, or influence over someone or something. When a person, idea, belief, or force "holds sway," it dominates — it shapes how people think, feel, or behave in a powerful and often widespread way.

Think of it like this: whoever or whatever "holds sway" is essentially in charge — not necessarily through laws or rules, but through deep influence or authority that others follow, accept, or submit to.

The key to understanding this idiom is the word "sway."

Physically, "sway" means to swing back and forth — like a tree branch swaying in the wind. The branch bends wherever the wind pushes it. This physical image gave birth to a figurative idea: if you can make things bend to your will, you have sway — you have influence and power.

Over centuries, "sway" became a word for rule or dominion, meaning the power to control or govern. So "hold sway" simply means to hold that power — to maintain a firm grip on influence or control.

The idiom has roots in Old English and Old Norse, where "sway" (from the Old Norse word sveigja, meaning "to bend or give way") gradually developed from a physical meaning into a figurative one connected to rulership and authority.

By the 16th century, "sway" was being used in English to mean dominion or rule — as in, a king who "holds sway" over his kingdom. The phrase has been a part of the English language ever since, surviving into modern usage especially in formal writing, journalism, literature, and speeches.

Structure:

The most common pattern is:

[Someone/Something] + holds sway + over + [a person, group, place, or situation]

The word "over" is very commonly used with this idiom, though it is not always required.

Here are examples across different contexts so you can see how flexible this idiom is:

About a person:

  • "For many years, the old general held sway over the entire military."

(= The general had powerful control over the military.)

About an idea or belief:

  • "In the 19th century, the belief that the Earth was only a few thousand years old still held sway among many people."

(= That belief was dominant and widely accepted.)

About an emotion:

  • "During the crisis, fear held sway over the whole nation."

(= Fear had a powerful grip on the nation; it dominated people's feelings and actions.)

About a trend or style:

  • "Before streaming services arrived, television held sway in every household."

(= Television was the dominant, most powerful form of entertainment.)

About a place:

  • "In this remote village, old traditions still hold sway."

(= Old traditions are still dominant and control how people live.)
Key Things to Understand About This Idiom

1. It implies strong, lasting, or widespread influence — not a small or temporary one.

"Hold sway" is not used for minor or fleeting influence. It suggests something that has serious power, often over a large group of people, a wide area, or a long period of time. You wouldn't say "his joke held sway over the room for a second." That's too small and brief. You'd say "his charisma held sway over the entire audience throughout his speech."

2. It can describe people, ideas, emotions, trends, forces — almost anything.

This is a very flexible idiom. The thing that "holds sway" doesn't have to be a person. It can be:

  • An ideology (e.g., democracy, religion)
  • An emotion (e.g., fear, love, hope)
  • A trend (e.g., a fashion, a technology)
